limitations.text: Cada fila es un informe registrado por una fuente, no un hecho verificado ni un avistamiento confirmado. Coincidir con Bronze no prueba que el relato sea verdadero.
Algunos informes tienen coincidencias por revisar con otros. No están confirmados como duplicados: cada uno cuenta como un informe.
Los eventos existen solo para los grupos de duplicados confirmados por coincidencia exacta. Los informes únicos y los candidatos pendientes no son eventos.
Solo informes con fecha apta para calendario; quedan fuera fechas calificadas, intervalos, faltantes, inválidas y en revisión.
Solo informes con mes fiable; quedan fuera las fechas de solo año y las 01-01 de fuentes con exceso de ese marcador.
Solo informes con día fiable; quedan fuera los días 01 y 15 de las fuentes con exceso de marcadores, además de las fechas de mes o año.
Solo informes con hora de minuto o mejor y fecha apta. Es hora local declarada sin zona horaria; muchas horas están redondeadas a la hora en punto.
Solo informes con coordenadas completas, en rango y fuera de cuarentena. Una coordenada puede ser el centro de una ciudad, no el lugar exacto del testigo.
Solo informes con país canónico consistente; los países contradictorios, históricos o no reconocidos quedan fuera.
La distancia es a la instalación más cercana del catálogo local de Silver (bases, laboratorios y polígonos), no a todas las instalaciones del mundo. Cercanía no implica relación.
Algunas fuentes usan días marcadores (01, 15 o 01-01) cuando no conocen la fecha exacta; Silver reduce la precisión de esos informes en lugar de inventar o borrar fechas.
Sentimiento, emociones, hoax_likelihood y quality_score son salidas de modelos o heurísticas heredadas del origen, no hechos ni verificaciones. No se presentan como verdad.
La cobertura depende de cada fuente y época: predominan los informes de Estados Unidos y de los años con sistemas de reporte en línea; NUFORC aparece en UFOCAT y en UPDB.
Parte de las coordenadas, países u horas procede del catálogo fijado de UFO-search y no de Bronze (uses_external_evidence=1).

1948 Aztec, New Mexico UFO Crash Retrieval

During Operation Laser Strike (Feb 1997), USMC Lance Corporal Jonathan Waygandt and fellow Marines reported encountering a crashed egg-shaped craft in the Peruvian jungle, described with a 'mother-of-pearl' skin. A subsequent Department of Energy retrieval team allegedly arrived to secure the site. JSOC / Special Operations Aviation Regiment helicopters are alleged to have provided logistics support.

Frank Scully introduced the Aztec case in his 1950 book Behind the Flying Saucers. Scully's primary sources (Silas Newton, Leo GeBauer) were later exposed as fraudsters. However, William Steinman and others later revisited the case with additional witness testimony, suggesting the original sources' fraud may have been an intelligence-community cover for a real event.

On April 11, 1980, Peruvian Air Force pilot Lt. Oscar Santa Maria Huertas intercepted a balloon-shaped object over La Joya Air Base. He fired 64 rounds of 30mm cannon at the object — which absorbed the rounds without damage. The object then accelerated to high altitude and disappeared. This is one of the few UAP intercept cases formally acknowledged by a national air force. No physical recovery occurred.

On April 17, 1897, the Dallas Morning News reported that an airship crashed into a windmill on the property of Judge J.S. Proctor in Aurora, Texas. The pilot — described as 'not of this world' — was reportedly killed and given a Christian burial in the local cemetery. Pieces of the craft were said to have been dumped into the well under the windmill.

On August 25, 1974, a UFO was tracked on radar intercepting USG territory about 40 mi southwest of Corpus Christi, Texas. The object reportedly collided with a small private aircraft (which departed El Paso International bound for Mexico City) over northern Mexico; both crashed in the desert near Coyame, Chihuahua. Mexican military responded first. Per Leonard Stringfield's sources and later testimony expanded in UAP Gerb's 2025 deep-dive, a US recovery team — staged at Fort Bliss and including Captain Lawrence Merley, Lieutenants Randall Bishop / Benjamin Rhodes / Jerome Smith, and Sergeant Terrence Miles — entered Mexico via UH-1 Huey helicopters (with or without authorization) and retrieved the disc. Cited as one of the earliest documented US cross-border crash-retrieval operations.

On December 9, 1965, a fireball was reported across at least six US states and Ontario; debris reportedly fell in the woods near Kecksburg, Pennsylvania. Multiple eyewitnesses — including volunteer fireman Jim Romanski, machinist Bill 'Bully' Bush, his cousin JS, journalist John Murphy (WHJB radio), state police fire marshal Carl Metz, and members of the Romansky family — described an acorn-shaped object the size of a Volkswagen Beetle, with bell-like / Liberty-Bell shape and hieroglyphic-like markings around its base. The U.S. military cordoned the area; a flatbed truck reportedly removed an object under tarp, allegedly routed via Lockbourne AFB to Wright-Patterson. The Air Force officially attributes the event to a meteor; researchers associate it with the Project Moondust recovery program with 'Blue Beret' Special Forces support.

On May 6, 1978, a large luminous object reportedly crashed on El Taire Mountain near the Bolivian-Argentine border. Both Bolivian and Argentine governments officially acknowledged the event. Declassified U.S. State Department cables (FOIA-released) document active US interest and a Project Moondust-style assessment. No public US recovery confirmation.

Per Philip J. Corso's testimony, during the October 26, 1962 Bluegill Triple Prime high-altitude nuclear test (the third successful redo of the Bluegill shot in Operation Fishbowl), a U.S. Navy recovery team retrieved what was initially described as a 'broken wiring harness' with each loose strand emitting a distinctive optical signature. The component was later allegedly identified as non-human technology and routed through the same legacy-program chain as Roswell material. Cited by Corso in the context of NHI surveillance of US high-altitude nuclear testing.

Per witness Debbie Clayton's testimony (surfaced via UAP Gerb's Edwards AFB Reverse Engineering Vol.2 video, 2025), an acorn-shaped craft crashed in broad daylight approximately 15 miles outside Edwards Air Force Base in 1971. Clayton and her girlfriend's family investigated the site, but USAF crews arrived within 15 minutes and secured the area. Morphology echoes the [[1965 Kecksburg UFO crash|1965 Kecksburg]] acorn-craft profile. Adds to the small but consistent set of California-desert crash retrievals associated with the Edwards / Plant 42 / Antelope Valley aerospace complex.

Reportedly contemporaneous with (or part of) the broader 1947 Roswell event. Engineer Grady L. 'Barney' Barnett claimed to have come upon a crashed disc on the Plains of San Agustin in early July 1947, encountering 4 small humanoid bodies and a group of archaeology students from the University of Pennsylvania. The case is the most-cited Roswell-adjacent crash claim and is sometimes presented as the actual Roswell crash site (vs. the Foster Ranch debris field).

Reportedly recovered during Operation Upshot Knothole nuclear-test series. USAF project engineer Arthur Stansel (later identified as 'Fitz Werner') described being part of a recovery team that retrieved a disc-shaped craft and one humanoid body. Bill Uhouse later claimed the craft was transported to Area 51 and the dead pilot to Los Alamos.

Reportedly the first 20th-century crash retrieval, allegedly recovered by Mussolini's Italian fascist government and studied under a secret investigation unit known as 'RS-33' (Reparto Studi 33). Documentary evidence emerged via researcher Roberto Pinotti in the late 1990s. Referenced by David Grusch in 2023 testimony as a confirmed case.

The 'Brazilian Roswell.' On January 20, 1996, multiple witnesses in Varginha reported encounters with small humanoid creatures with red eyes. The creatures were allegedly apprehended by Brazilian military and transported to medical facilities; at least one reportedly died in custody. Recovery participant Sgt. Marco Eli Cherese died from infection a month later — paralleling US witness-illness claims.

The most famous UFO crash case in history. In early July 1947, debris was recovered from a ranch near Roswell, New Mexico. The Roswell Army Air Field issued a press release on July 8 confirming recovery of a 'flying disc'; the Army retracted within hours, claiming the debris was a weather balloon (later attributed to Project Mogul). Multiple military and civilian witnesses have since described unusual debris materials and small humanoid bodies.

1st Lt David H. Schuur, Deputy Commander at the Echo Launch Control Capsule of the 455th/91st Strategic Missile Wing at Minot AFB, reported that during a 1966 alert tour a large bright object systematically traversed the entire Minuteman missile wing from southeast to northwest (Alpha through Oscar flights), appearing to 'scan each missile, one by one.' As the object approached Echo Flight, Schuur's crew received 'spurious indicators — anomalous readings,' culminating in 'Launch in Progress!' indicators on approximately 6-8 of the 10 missiles. Schuur had to activate the Inhibit switch to prevent automatic launch sequencing. Predates the March 1967 Echo/Oscar Flight events by ~7 months.

A3C Gary L. Ames of the 42nd Combat Defense Squadron observed a dark, flat-panelled object ~25-30 feet wide and 10 feet tall hovering 2-3 feet above the ground about 500 yards south of the runway at Loring AFB, October–November 1964. A violet glow was visible from the object's underside through his pocket scope. A second airman ~100 yards closer confirmed the sighting; the object departed 'so fast as to be a blur' when the patrol vehicle approached. Both witnesses were ordered by a senior colonel never to discuss the incident. Precedes the famous 1975 Loring UFO flap by over a decade.

An unidentified object was observed hovering over an Atlas F missile silo at Walker AFB in October 1963. Security Alert Team dispatched to investigate. Object departed vertically at high speed. Walker's 579th Strategic Missile Squadron operated 12 Atlas F ICBMs at the time.

August 1976 overflight of Cannon AFB, then home to nuclear-capable F-111 aircraft. Multiple security personnel reported the low-altitude hovering object; radar returns were briefly logged before the object departed vertically.
August 1994 Security Alert Team response to multiple inner-zone perimeter alarms at a Minot AFB Minuteman III launch facility, with a visual UAP encountered on approach.

Beginning December 5, 1948, a wave of green-incandescent fireballs — behaving like slow, horizontal, silent, unexploded meteor-like objects — was observed repeatedly over Los Alamos, Sandia, and Kirtland AFB. Meteoricist Lincoln La Paz concluded they were not natural meteors. The USAF established Project Twinkle (1949–1951) specifically to investigate the wave, which targeted U.S. nuclear weapons development and storage infrastructure.

Between October 27 and 31, 1975, unidentified helicopter-like objects repeatedly penetrated the Loring AFB nuclear weapons storage area perimeter at low altitude. The 42nd Bombardment Wing declared Security Option 3. FAA, Canadian authorities, and NORAD were alerted. No conventional helicopter source was identified. The event kicked off the 1975 SAC base flap — nearly identical incursions occurred at Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, and Minot over the following two weeks.

Between September 1983 and mid-1984, multiple Minuteman III launch facilities at F.E. Warren AFB reported UAP visits concurrent with perimeter alarm activations. F.E. Warren was then host to the majority of the USAF's operational ICBM inventory.

Between September 19–21, 2012, multiple civilians within the Malmstrom AFB Minuteman III missile field reported V-shaped and bar-shaped objects with orange lights near the Oscar-01 and Delta-01 Missile Alert Facilities. Jennifer Styer's initial sighting was logged at the Fergus County Sheriff's Office at 22:19 on Sep 19. Malmstrom AFB officially stated no aircraft operations near the sighting locations. Residents reported increased Air Force security patrols and missile maintenance van activity in subsequent weeks.

During November 7–10, 1975, Malmstrom AFB launch facilities reported repeated UAP visits at low altitude over Minuteman III silos. F-106 interceptors from Great Falls were scrambled multiple nights. The objects outpaced the F-106s vertically and laterally. NORAD radar corroborated the ground sightings. One missile — K-7 — reportedly suffered guidance system anomalies during this period.

During a September 15, 1964 Atlas F dummy-warhead test shot from Vandenberg, a tracking telescope at Big Sur — operated by 1st Lt Robert Jacobs's crew — filmed a disc-shaped object that approached the warhead, fired four beams of light at it from four points around its rim, and departed. The warhead malfunctioned and fell into the Pacific short of its target. The film was confiscated by unknown officers at the Big Sur facility.
February 1968 UAP visit to the Oscar-07 Minuteman I launch facility at Minot AFB, correlating with inner-zone perimeter alarm activations.

July 1963 UAP observed over the White Sands Missile Range — a facility central to U.S. missile test and early-atomic development dating back to Trinity (1945). Photos were taken but reportedly classified.
July 1977 UAP hovering reported near a Minuteman II launch facility at Ellsworth AFB, then operated by the 44th Strategic Missile Wing.

Just days after Loring, identical low-altitude penetrations of the Wurtsmith AFB nuclear weapons storage area began on October 30, 1975. A KC-135 tanker was scrambled and tracked the object on radar as it paced the aircraft — eventually departing at high speed.

Late 1998: Christopher Cabrera, a Nellis AFB Security Forces member (1998-2002), observed three extremely bright amber lights in a vertical triangular arrangement ~100 feet above ground and ¼ mile from his southwest-perimeter patrol position at Area 2 (Nellis's nuclear weapons storage area). The lights blinked sequentially (apex, then bottom-left, then bottom-right) for ~10 seconds, fading in-and-out, completely silent. The object 'blocked out the stars behind it,' indicating a single solid craft rather than separate lights. Control Center halted all patrol movements and dispatched an Oscar perimeter team. All witnesses were instructed by the Flight Chief that the incident 'never happened' and threatened with dishonorable discharge for disclosure.

Late fall 1986: Joseph C. Pscolka Jr., former USAF Security Policeman serving as Alpha-1 Flight Security Controller (10th Strategic Missile Squadron), reported observing five lights above the Alpha-1 Missile Alert Facility at Malmstrom AFB. Five additional lights descended from the clouds and joined the first five, after which all ten 'maneuvered like nothing manmade could have' — high-speed darting, sharp-angle turns, 'like crazy fireflies for about a minute' — before descending near ground level and zipping off in all directions. Pscolka was interrogated the next morning by the Wing Commander and Security Police Group Commander; all witnesses were required to sign non-disclosure agreements.

Multiple 1950 sightings over the Hanford plutonium production reservation prompted F-82 Twin Mustang interceptor scrambles. Objects consistently outperformed the interceptors. AEC and USAF documented the encounters internally; Hanford was then the sole U.S. plutonium source.
Multiple security personnel at Minot AFB's Minuteman I launch facilities reported low-altitude overflights by unidentified objects in August 1966, coinciding with unusual radar returns.
October 1969 UAP overflight of the Minot AFB B-52 nuclear alert aircraft parking area. Security personnel reported a silent low-altitude object.

On August 8–9, 1980, a series of UAP incidents at Kirtland AFB culminated with an object reportedly landing inside the [[Manzano Weapons Storage Area]]. An official AFOSI Complaint Form 4 documenting the event was later released via FOIA. Signed by [[Richard Doty]] — subsequently a figure in separate UAP-related counterintelligence controversies.

On March 16, 1967, all 10 Minuteman I ICBMs of Echo Flight at Malmstrom AFB went simultaneously off-alert (guidance-and-control no-go). Security teams had reported a UAP hovering above the launch facility shortly before the event. A second shutdown at Oscar Flight followed a week later. Captain Robert Salas, the Oscar Flight deputy missile combat crew commander, became the most-cited public witness. FOIA documents corroborate the simultaneous no-go event.

On March 24, 1967 — approximately a week after Echo Flight — Oscar Flight at Malmstrom AFB suffered a similar simultaneous missile shutdown. Capt Robert Salas was the deputy missile combat crew commander. Security reports again described an unidentified object hovering over the launch facility prior to the missiles going offline.

On November 11, 1975 — concurrent with the U.S. SAC base flap — Canadian Forces Station Falconbridge (a NORAD radar site) tracked a UAP performing extreme altitude changes (surface to 72,000 feet) while appearing stationary visually. One of the best radar-confirmed cases of the era, with the added significance of coinciding exactly with the cross-continent SAC flap.

On November 25, 1982, U.S. Army MP Christopher Grooms (Tower 5, 558th Military Police Company) observed a dark triangular craft that 'absorbed light rather than reflected it' traverse slowly northeast for 7-10 minutes directly over the Kriegsfeld Army Special Weapons Depot in Rhineland-Palatinate, West Germany. As the craft passed overhead, Grooms witnessed it perform a 360-degree nose-down roll while maintaining forward momentum — a maneuver 'no aircraft could do.' He experienced tunnel vision and a sense of being 'acknowledged' by the occupants. Grooms did not report the incident at the time due to security clearance concerns; disclosed publicly decades later.

On November 4, 1957, an egg-shaped object was observed hovering low over the [[Manzano Weapons Storage Area]] at Kirtland AFB. Two CAA tower controllers and base personnel witnessed the object for ~20 minutes. The case became one of the strongest Project Blue Book files involving a nuclear storage area.

On October 23, 2010, 50 Minuteman III ICBMs — one full missile squadron — at F.E. Warren AFB lost status-monitoring communication with their Launch Control Center for approximately 45 minutes. The USAF acknowledged the event publicly; official cause given was a faulty circuit card. Hastings' sources — active-duty USAF personnel and a retired missile maintenance technician — independently reported a 'huge' cigar-shaped craft resembling a WWI-era Zeppelin (~7:1 length-to-width ratio, dull grey) sighted near the affected missile field on Oct 23–24. Hastings emphasizes his sources have not claimed the UAP caused the disruption — only that the UAP was present during it. Multiple civilians in adjacent Nebraska/Wyoming/Colorado counties reported dome-shaped, cylindrical, and triangular craft across Sep 2010–Feb 2011, many within the FE Warren missile field footprint.

On October 24, 1968, a B-52 aircrew returning to Minot AFB tracked a UAP on air radar while ground launch-control facilities simultaneously reported visual sightings of a large object near Minuteman missile silos. The Project Blue Book file remains one of the most thoroughly-documented UAP-nuclear cases — air radar + ground radar + multiple visual witnesses.

On October 4, 1989, Soviet strategic missile forces at Byelokoroviche reported a UAP hovering above a Topol ICBM launch facility. Launch status indicators briefly entered launch commit sequence before autonomously standing down. Later disclosed in the Soviet MoD's 1990s UFO file release — treated as the Soviet analog to the 1967 Malmstrom Echo Flight incident.

Over three nights in January 1945, Lt. JG Clarence R. 'Bud' Clem attempted night interceptions in an F6F Hellcat of an unidentified object — described as a 'huge fireball' — that maneuvered above the Hanford plutonium-production plant. The object was radar-tracked but repeatedly evaded the Hellcat. This is the earliest known documented UAP-nuclear encounter, preceding the Roswell era by 2½ years and occurring mid-Manhattan Project.
Pre-Echo Flight UAP visits to Malmstrom Minuteman launch facilities during 1966, setting the pattern for the March 1967 simultaneous-shutdown event.

Shortly after a French atomic test in the early 1960s (France tested at Reggane, Algeria 1960–1961), A3C Larry W. Rogers and five others of the USAF 3926th Air Police Squadron K-9 observed approximately a half-dozen small glowing objects hovering above the Atlas Mountains ~90 miles southeast of Ben Guerir Air Base. When four-to-five F-100 jet fighters scrambled from Zaragoza AB (Spain), the objects performed sharp-angled evasive turns 'like playing tag with the jets' for ~45 minutes. All witnesses were debriefed individually, shown AFR 200-2, and required to sign non-disclosure statements.

The Soviet Kapustin Yar missile test range reported multiple UAP encounters during 1982. Declassified KGB UFO files (released in the 1990s) document radar-confirmed intrusions by objects performing maneuvers beyond then-known Soviet or U.S. aircraft capability.

The final leg of the 1975 SAC base flap: starting around November 10, 1975, Minot AFB reported low-altitude UAP visits to both B-52 nuclear bomber areas and Minuteman III launch facilities — the same pattern that had traveled from Loring → Wurtsmith → Malmstrom → Minot in ~14 days.

Within a few months of the 1964 Ames sighting, an unnamed Air Policeman at a rear guard position near a nuclear-armed B-52 alert pad at Loring AFB reported encountering 'two little grey men.' The airman fired a warning shot and then fired directly on the figures. He was immediately relieved of duty and his account initially dismissed as sleepwalking, though he maintained its veracity for the rest of his career. Name withheld by Hastings at witness request.
